transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-03-22 16:30 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Priya (Redwood AE), Marco (Redwood SE), Lena (Redwood CSM), Elaine (Argento Head of ML), Jordan (CTO), Samir (SRE), Maya (Product)

Summary (auto): quick notes on pricing levers and pilot next steps.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Priya (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for doing this. we want to make sure we map cost to the things you care about — latency, predictable monthly burn, and data residency. can you help me frame where you're at?
[00:25] Elaine (Argento - Head of ML): yeah thanks, priya. our main use case today is a multimodal assistant for logistics planners — so lots of short prompts, some longer explanation requests. we estimate 12M tokens / month initially but with spikes. budget is... tight. target is to not exceed ~USD 8k/mo for inference ideally.
[00:46] Jordan (CTO): and also two anchor flows where latency matters — the planner UI needs responses under 300ms p95. other flows can tolerate up to 1s.
[01:05] Priya (Redwood AE): ok that helps. quick clarifying Q: are you currently running any LLMs in-house or using a hosted provider?
[01:12] Samir (SRE): we have some fine-tuned models on prem but throughput is low; most production traffic we've been routing to a managed API (not naming) but the cost scaled badly when we increased fan-out.
[01:25] Marco (Redwood SE): right — so the tradeoffs we'll talk about are per-token rate, batching/caching opportunities, and the hosting mix (hosted vs dedicated vs private). i want to call out a couple concepts up front: prefix caching (we call it prefix cache/KV cache), and continuous batching. those are the big levers to reduce per-token spend without impacting tail latency too much.
[01:52] Maya (Product): can you give a simple example of what that saves? numbers help us sell this internally.
[01:58] Marco (Redwood SE): sure — for a short-chat style turn average 25 tokens you might see hosted per-token baseline X. with prefix caching for repeated prefixes (like system prompts + user profile) you can cut effective generation tokens by up to 40-60% depending on repetition. continuous batching helps amortize fixed per-request overhead — that's more helpful for high QPS patterns.
[02:25] Elaine: so caching needs us to have repeated prefixes — our planner does reuse the same templates a lot, yes.
[02:31] Priya: okay good signal. budget around 8k/mo, 12M tokens — i want to sketch a rough hosted estimate now just to check if it's in the ballpark. this is high-level.
[02:45] [00:03:00] Priya: if we assume hosted list price 0.0008 per token (example), 12M tokens would be 9.6k — slightly over. but with caching and batching we often see 30-50% effective token reduction so you land under 8k. for the latency-critical 300ms path we might recommend dedicated slots to guarantee p95.
[03:20] Jordan: dedicated is more expensive in absolute dollars but gives you predictability?
[03:26] Marco: exactly. Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools. you pay for reserved capacity (committed monthly) but your per-token marginal cost drops and tail latencies tighten. hosted is pay-as-you-go with quick scale but less predictability under burst.
[03:45] Samir: what about private/VPC? we have regulatory noise in a couple of clients — we may need a VPC deployment with our KMS.
[03:54] Priya: private is an option. it's a bit of a lift to onboard but we support customer-managed KMS and audit logs. it typically shifts to a license plus infra arrangement.
[04:10] [00:05:00] Elaine: ok what's the typical pilot route? start hosted then move to dedicated? or start dedicated?
[04:18] Priya: common pattern: pilot on hosted (low time-to-value), tune batching/caching and run bench. if you need consistent latency for specific flows, pilot a small dedicated pool in parallel — or do a short eval where we simulate your QPS on dedicated to compare tail.
[04:38] Marco: and we'll run your sample prompts to measure effective token reduction from prefix/KV cache and show per-call latency under our batching policies. that gives you concrete unit economics to take to finance.
[04:55] Maya: what about burst capacity? our peaks are unpredictable.
[05:00] Marco: hosted supports autoscaling and burst, dedicated has burst credits and configured overflow to hosted (if you want both). there's also a routing policy: route latency-critical traffic to dedicated and background tasks to hosted.
[05:20] Jordan: what's the SLA difference?
[05:23] Priya: dedicated customers get SLA-backed uptime and defined latency targets per deployment class. hosted has best-effort latency SLAs but we provide SLO monitoring and alerts.
[05:35] [00:08:00] Elaine: curious about upfront commitment for dedicated — how long is typical and can we do a small commit to start?
[05:43] Priya: yes — you can do a small committed capacity monthly and scale. many customers do 3–6 month pilots with a smaller commit.
[05:52] Samir: can we talk tech — the prefix cache — does it keep KV cache per customer or per model shard?
[05:58] Marco: good question. we maintain per-customer KV cache keyed by model version+request prefix signature; it lives in memory on serving nodes and is safe to evict under memory pressure. for private deployments we provide that same behavior but managed inside your VPC.
[06:20] Elaine: if the cache is per-customer does it increase memory footprint linearly with customers?
[06:25] Marco: yes but it's bounded — we shard caches across GPUs and have eviction policies; practically it's not a linear explosion for common patterns. we'll share some numbers from similar customers.
[06:40] [00:10:00] Maya: okay — one of our constraints is finance wants a per-2-week predictable budget lane, not a wildly fluctuating bill. is there a way to carve that?
[06:50] Priya: yes — you can combine reserved capacity with usage alerts and billing buckets. we can create sub-accounts and route specific endpoints to a reserved pool so their charge is fixed-ish. the rest can be pay-as-you-go.
[07:12] Jordan: example: if we reserve two GPUs for the 300ms flow, can we estimate the monthly committed cost vs hosted?
[07:20] Marco: rough numbers: a small dedicated pool (equivalent to 2xA100 class) might be $6–9k/mo committed depending on GPU generation and discounts. that gives you predictable latency and throughput. hosted to handle the rest might be another 2–3k depending on effective tokens after cache. so combined could sit near your 8k target if caching reduces token consumption.
[07:52] Elaine: that's tighter than I expected. do you have examples where customers hit the 40% token reduction?
[07:58] Marco: yes for templated assistant flows where system prompt + user profile is repeated. for free-text search-style queries the savings are lower. we will test with your 500 samples.
[08:14] [00:13:00] Priya: are there any constraints we should know — compliance, data residency — that change the hosting recommendation?
[08:20] Samir: we have a couple enterprise clients in EMEA asking for data not to cross certain regions. also internal security wants SSO + audit logs.
[08:29] Priya: fine — for residency you can pin deployments to regions; private/VPC is the strictest option. for SSO we integrate with Okta/SAML and we provide audit logs for both hosted and dedicated.
[08:44] Maya: about model choice — do you host our fine-tuned weights? we need to avoid exporting their customer PII into another vendor's environment.
[08:52] Marco: we support private model onboarding — for hosted we can accept customer-owned models with an NDA/process or suggest using Redwood-managed variants. for private deployments you bring the model artifact inside your VPC.
[09:08] Elaine: what about model quantization? we were told that lower precision can save compute but impact accuracy.
[09:14] Marco: yes — quantization reduces memory and infer cost; we recommend eval-driven quantization. our Optimize tooling suggests quant profiles by workload and flags regressions. during the pilot we'll show quality tradeoffs.
[09:30] [00:16:00] Jordan: ok i want to pin down success criteria for the pilot — finance accepts if unit cost < $0.0006/token effective for the 12M projection and p95 latency for critical flow < 300ms. also need security pack.
[09:45] Priya: noted. we'll run bench and produce a per-route cost sheet that maps to those KPIs.
[09:52] Maya: timeline — how fast can we run the bench?
[09:56] Marco: if you provide sample prompts and peak QPS shape by Thursday, we can run a bench and send results in ~4 business days.
[10:06] Elaine: we can do that. Samir will drop the traffic pattern doc.
[10:10] Samir: will do.
[10:14] [00:19:00] Priya: quick aside — competitors, do you currently have pricing comparisons?
[10:19] Jordan: we tested a handful — one was more expensive at scale, another had better latencies but poor caching support.
[10:27] Priya: ok — we'll include a short competitive snapshot in the follow-up.
[10:32] Maya: any gotchas re. logs and redaction? we need to ensure PII is redacted before being stored.
[10:38] Marco: we provide configurable retention and optional token-level redaction; for dedicated/private you can enforce zero retention. we'll send the security pack with details.
[10:52] [00:22:00] Elaine: pricing model detail question — is the hosted price strictly per-input+output tokens? or are there connection/overhead fees?
[10:58] Priya: hosted is primarily per-token for generation and separate per-embedding units. minimal request overhead fees are baked into the model rate; for premium features like extended retention or high-frequency AX slots there can be add-ons. we'll detail those in the quote.
[11:12] Jordan: can we set per-route budgets so product owners can't overspend?
[11:16] Priya: yes — console can put quotas per API key/route and alert owners when thresholds hit.
[11:22] Samir: for the pilot, we want deterministic small bill — can Redwood issue an estimate invoice?
[11:27] Priya: we can produce a pilot pricing spreadsheet that models committed vs usage for the 3-month window. that will be the next step.
[11:36] [00:26:00] Marco: technical note — when we report token reduction from cache, we'll show two numbers: raw tokens avoided (savings) and effective per-call latency impact. sometimes cache improves cost but hurts warm-start latency if cache miss patterns are high. we'll surface that.
[11:54] Elaine: helpful. also curious about batching — we are concerned batching will add too much latency to the 300ms flow.
[12:02] Marco: continuous batching can be tuned — we can use per-route batching windows. critical route can use immediate mode (no batching or tiny micro-batches) and still get KV cache benefits. less critical routes get larger batches for cost efficiency.
[12:20] Maya: great. let's talk deliverables — what will Redwood send after this call?
[12:24] Priya: three artifacts: 1) pilot pricing spreadsheet (hosted vs hosted+dedicated), 2) security pack + SOC2 summary, 3) benchmark run plan.
[12:34] Jordan: and a proposed pilot timeline?
[12:36] Priya: yes — we'll propose a 6-week pilot: week 1 onboarding and data collection, week 2 bench runs, week 3-4 tuning and configuration, week 5 reporting, week 6 optional buffer and exec review.
[12:50] [00:30:00] Elaine: on the bench data — we will share 500 canonical prompts and a 2-week QPS shape. do you need more?
[12:57] Marco: that's enough to start. if you have edge-case long prompts include ~50 longer examples.
[13:06] Samir: any hidden charges for egress or data transfer?
[13:10] Priya: in hosted egress is typical cloud egress; for dedicated/private we can localize region to minimize egress. we'll call out any egress in the quote.
[13:24] Maya: ok timeline for docs?
[13:27] Priya: we'll send the pack and pricing by Friday; bench results after we get prompts.
[13:32] [00:34:00] Jordan: one last question — if we later need private for compliance, how painful is the migration?
[13:39] Marco: migration is straightforward conceptually: redeploy the same serving configs to your VPC, bring model artifacts, and cut over traffic. there is some lead time for network setup and KMS integration (2–4 weeks typically). we'll help with runbook.
[13:54] Elaine: that's acceptable.
[13:58] Priya: sweet. i'm going to recap quickly and nail down owners. recap: Priya sends pricing & security pack; Marco runs bench once prompts/QPS in; Elaine/Samir provide prompts + traffic doc; next sync after bench results. any objections?
[14:18] Maya: none.
[14:21] Jordan: sounds good.
[14:24] [00:38:00] Priya: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the materials and calendar invite for the bench run review.
[14:30] Elaine: thanks all.
[14:32] Samir: thanks.
[14:35] Marco: thanks everyone.

--- End transcript ---
